notes.meaning: Jesus and His followers were coming near to Jerusalem and stopped near the Mount of Olives. Even though He knew suffering and arrest were waiting for Him in the city, He chose to make an open and public arrival. He sent two disciples ahead into a nearby village with special instructions.

Jesus told the two disciples where to find a mother donkey and her young colt. He gave them exact directions before they even arrived, showing that nothing was hidden from His sight. They were to untie both animals and bring them to Him right away.

Jesus knew that people might ask why the animals were being taken. He told the disciples to say that the Lord needed them, promising that the owner would willingly let them go. Jesus showed His royal authority while still acting with complete honesty toward the owner.

Long before this day, the prophet Zechariah wrote that Jerusalem's true King would arrive gently, riding on a donkey rather than a warrior's horse. Jesus carried out this prophecy step by step to prove that He was the promised Messiah. He entered not with earthly pride or weapons of war, but with peace and humility to bring salvation.

The disciples trusted Jesus and did exactly what He told them to do. They did not argue or worry about being accused of theft, but went forward in simple obedience. When God gives a command, He prepares the way for His people to carry it out.

The disciples brought the animals and placed their outer cloaks on them to serve as a saddle. Jesus then sat upon the garments on the colt to ride toward the city. The humble setup matched His mission as a gentle King who did not seek worldly luxury.

A large crowd honored Jesus by spreading their outer cloaks across the dirt road like a royal carpet. Others cut leafy branches from nearby trees and laid them down as a sign of joy and celebration. These common people gladly offered what they had to welcome Him as King.

The crowds ahead and behind Jesus cheered using words from Psalm 118, shouting 'Hosanna,' which means 'Save now, please!' They hailed Him as the Son of David, which was a special title for the promised Savior. They rejoiced that God was sending His King to bring peace and rescue His people.

When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the entire city was shaken with excitement and curiosity. People were startled by the loud crowds and wondered who this new arrival could be. Some welcomed Him with joy, while the religious rulers watched with growing jealousy and alarm.

The crowd answered the city's questions by identifying Jesus as the prophet from the town of Nazareth in Galilee. He had become famous throughout the land for His powerful teaching and miracles. Although He was born in Bethlehem, most people still knew Him by His childhood home.

Jesus entered the temple courtyards and drove out the merchants who were buying and selling animals for sacrifices. He overturned the tables of men exchanging money for the temple tax and knocked over the seats of bird sellers. He took action against the noise, cheating, and greed that had ruined God's holy place.

Jesus reminded the crowd that Scripture called God's temple a house of prayer for all people. Instead of honoring that holy purpose, greedy traders and corrupt priests had turned the outer courts into a hideout for thieves. True worship cannot live alongside dishonesty disguised as religion.

After clearing out the dishonest sellers, Jesus welcomed the blind and the lame into the temple courts and healed them. Those who were hurt and needy found mercy where merchants had sought only profit. These miraculous healings proved that He was truly the Messiah sent by God.

The chief priests and religious teachers were furious when they saw the miracles Jesus performed. They became even angrier when they heard children in the temple courts shouting praises to Him as the Son of David. Their pride and envy blinded them to the wonderful work of God happening right before their eyes.

The religious leaders demanded to know if Jesus heard what the children were shouting. Jesus answered by quoting Psalm 8, pointing out that God has planned for young children and nursing babies to offer perfect praise. When proud leaders refuse to give God glory, He often receives it from the humble and small.

Jesus left the city and walked about two miles to the quiet village of Bethany, where He spent the night. He stepped away from His angry enemies to rest and pray in peace. Throughout this final week, He returned to Bethany each evening before heading back to the temple.

Early the next morning, as Jesus walked back toward Jerusalem, He was hungry. This shows that He truly took on human nature, experiencing ordinary physical needs like hunger and tiredness. He remained completely devoted to His Father's work even while lacking food.

Spotting a fig tree covered with leaves along the road, Jesus went to see if it had fruit, but found none. Because a fig tree with leaves normally already has early fruit, this tree made a false promise. Jesus sentenced the tree never to produce fruit again, and it withered away right away as a warning against empty spiritual show.

The disciples were amazed when they saw how quickly the fig tree had dried up and died. They asked Jesus how such a sudden withering could happen. The sudden death of the tree showed the disciples the awesome power of the Lord's word.

Jesus told His disciples that if they had true faith without wavering, they could do far greater things than drying up a tree. Using a common Jewish saying, He explained that faith could even tell a mountain to be thrown into the sea. Trusting God's promises helps believers overcome seemingly impossible obstacles in their work for Him.

Jesus gave a reassuring promise that whatever believers ask for in prayer, believing, they will receive. Genuine faith does not make selfish demands, but looks to God with complete trust according to His will. Prayer and faith work together as the heart of a Christian's life.

When Jesus returned to the temple courts to teach, the chief priests and elders confronted Him to challenge His right to be there. They asked who gave Him the right to cleanse the courts and teach the people without their permission. Because they cared only about protecting their own authority, they refused to recognize God's hand at work in Him.
